paper_context.research_question: Do current language and vision (LaVi) models truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between the two modalities?
main_claims: Current state-of-the-art Language and Vision (LaVi) models do not truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between language and vision.
The proposed FOIL-COCO dataset, an extension of MS-COCO with correct and 'foil' captions (single-word mistakes), effectively challenges state-of-the-art LaVi models.

Current LaVi models perform poorly on three proposed tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction) on FOIL-COCO, often close to chance level, while humans achieve near-perfect performance.

LaVi models exhibit specific failures: coarse representations of language and visual input, insufficient fine-grained language representation for mismatch detection, and poor visual representation for correcting foil words.
LaVi models are biased towards frequently occurring concepts and struggle to distinguish related concepts when foil words are semantically similar to original words.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Novelty and utility of the FOIL-COCO dataset and its associated diagnostic tasks.
Rigour and clarity of the dataset generation methodology, including bias mitigation strategies.
Soundness and comprehensiveness of the experimental evaluation of state-of-the-art LaVi models.
Depth and insightfulness of the diagnostic analysis of model failures.
Clarity and reproducibility of the experimental setup and results.
Significance of findings for advancing research in fine-grained Language and Vision understanding.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art Language and Vision (LaVi) models do not truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between language and vision.
evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

We demonstrate that using language cues only is not enough to deal with FOIL-COCO and that it challenges the state-of-the-art by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image.
We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The state-of-the art LaVi models we have tested fall through that test, implying that they fail to integrate the two modalities.
uncertainty_flags: it remains unclear how the reported results should be interpreted and what those models are actually learning.
it is unclear whether they capture vision and language in a truly integrative fashion.

extracted_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO dataset challenges SOTA LaVi models
extracted_claims.claim_text: The proposed FOIL-COCO dataset, an extension of MS-COCO with correct and 'foil' captions (single-word mistakes), effectively challenges state-of-the-art LaVi models by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image.
evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

Our paper contributes to investigate these three weaknesses of current VQA and IC research by proposing an automatic method for creating a big dataset of real images with minimal language bias and some diagnostic abilities.
The dataset presented in this paper (Section 3) is built on top of MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014), and contains 297,268 datapoints and 97,847 images.
FOIL-COCO dataset is challenging.

extracted_claims.claim_label: LaVi models perform poorly on FOIL-COCO tasks
extracted_claims.claim_text: Current LaVi models perform poorly on three proposed tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction) on FOIL-COCO, often close to chance level, while humans achieve near-perfect performance.
evidence: We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The two state-of-the-art systems do significantly worse than humans on both T1 and T2.
They respectively only identify 34.51% (LSTM +norm I) and 36.38% (HieCoAtt) of the incorrect captions (T1).
On the foil word detection task, they only reach 24.25% and 33.69% accuracy (T2).
Their accuracy on foil word correction (T3) is extremely low, at 4.7% and 4.21% respectively.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Specific failures of LaVi models identified
extracted_claims.claim_text: LaVi models exhibit specific failures: coarse representations of language and visual input, insufficient fine-grained language representation for mismatch detection, and poor visual representation for correcting foil words.
evidence: First, their coarse representations of language and visual input do not encode suitably structured information to spot mismatches between an utterance and the corresponding scene (tested by T1).
Second, their language representation is not fine-grained enough to identify the part of an utterance that causes a mismatch with the image as it is (T2).
Third, their visual representation is also too poor to spot and name the visual area that corresponds to a marked mistake in the text (T3).
The result on T3 makes it clear that systems are unable to extract from the image representation the information needed to correct the foil.

extracted_claims.claim_label: LaVi models biased towards frequent/similar concepts
extracted_claims.claim_text: LaVi models are biased towards frequently occurring concepts and struggle to distinguish related concepts when foil words are semantically similar to original words.
evidence: When the foil word (e.g. cat) is semantically very similar to the original one (e.g. dog), the models tend to wrongly classify the caption as ‘correct’.
The same holds for frequency values. In particular, the higher the frequency of both the original word and the foil one, the more the models fail.

This indicates that systems find it difficult to distinguish related concepts at the text-vision interface, and also that they may tend to be biased towards frequently occurring concepts, ‘seeing them everywhere’ even when they are not present in the image.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Existing LaVi datasets have biases and conflate errors
extracted_claims.claim_text: Current Language and Vision (LaVi) datasets, such as VQA and IC, suffer from language priors, dataset biases, and conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses.
evidence: Such results indicate that in current datasets, language provides priors that make it possible for a LaVi model to be successful without truly understanding and integrating language and vision.
Johnson et al. (2016) highlight a second weakness of such datasets, pointing out that “they conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses”.

Recent work has shown that the LaVi models are mainly based on language priors (Ren et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2016; Kafle and Kanan, 2016) and even simple correlation and memorization (Zhou et al., 2015; Jabri et al., 2016; Hodosh and Hockenmaier, 2016) can result in a good superficial performance, without the underlying models truly understanding the visual content.

Zhang et al. (2016) first unveiled that there exists a huge dataset bias in the popular VQA dataset by Antol et al. (2015): they showed that almost half of all the questions in this dataset can be answered correctly by using the question alone and ignoring the image completely.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Existing IC evaluation metrics are inadequate
extracted_claims.claim_text: Existing Image Captioning (IC) evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap, are only weakly correlated with human judgments, and fail to capture semantic propositional content.
evidence: it has been observed that existing IC evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap and that there is a need for measures that better substitute human judgments (Hodosh et al., 2013; Elliott and Keller, 2014; Anderson et al., 2016).

Elliott and Keller (2014) performed a sentence-level correlation analysis of NLG evaluation measures against expert human judgements in the context of IC. Their study revealed that most of those metrics were only weakly correlated with human judgements.
Anderson et al. (2016) showed that the most widely-used metrics for IC fail to capture semantic propositional content, which is an essential component of human caption evaluation.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO dataset generation process, particularly the mining of the hardest foil caption using Neuraltalk, minimizes visual-language dataset bias.
evidence: To eliminate possible visual-language dataset bias, for each image and original caption, out of all foil captions generated in step 3, we selected only the hardest one.

We use Neuraltalk proposed in (Fei-Fei, 2015), one of the state-of-the-art image captioning systems, pre-trained on MS-COCO. Neuraltalk is based on an LSTM which takes as input an image and generates a sentence describing its content. We obtain a neural network N that implicitly represents the visual-language bias in its weights.
The ‘blind’, language-only model does badly on T1 with an accuracy of 43.95% (19.53% on foil captions), demonstrating that language bias is minimal.

extracted_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive for humans
extracted_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive to human beings, as evidenced by near-perfect human performance and simple annotation instructions.
evidence: We note as well that our task does not require any complex instructions for the annotation, indicating that it is intuitive to human beings (see §4).
Annotators are nearly perfect in classifying captions and detecting foil words.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The ability to 'truly grasp the interaction' between modalities implies achieving human-level performance on diagnostic tasks like FOIL-COCO.
supporting_evidence: Humans, in contrast, have near-perfect performance on those tasks.
We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately.
Annotators are nearly perfect in classifying captions and detecting foil words.
Our hypothesis is that systems which, like humans, deeply integrate the language and vision modalities, should spot foil captions quite easily.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The interpretation of model failures as a lack of 'true understanding' might be overstated if human performance is not a suitable benchmark or if the tasks test a different cognitive ability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Introducing a single-word error ('foil') per caption is a sufficient and effective method to test fine-grained interaction between language and vision.
supporting_evidence: We only introduce one error (or ‘foil’) per caption (i.e. the caption is ‘nearly’ correct).
In contrast, the foil captions we propose only differ from the gold description by one word and are thus more challenging.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If models can handle single-word errors but fail on other types of fine-grained mismatches, the diagnostic power of FOIL-COCO might be limited to this specific error type.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Replacing nouns from the same MS-COCO supercategory creates semantically challenging and relevant foil words for diagnostic purposes.
supporting_evidence: We take target and foil words to be nouns, specifically the labels of MS-COCO categories, and we couple together words belonging to the same supercategory (e.g., bicycle::motorcycle, bicycle::car, bird::dog).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the chosen supercategory pairings do not consistently produce challenging foils, or if they introduce unintended biases, the diagnostic insights might be skewed.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Neuraltalk's loss function, when pre-trained on MS-COCO, accurately models the visual-language bias of the dataset and can reliably identify the 'hardest' foil captions.
supporting_evidence: To this end, we use Neuraltalk proposed in (Fei-Fei, 2015), one of the state-of-the-art image captioning systems, pre-trained on MS-COCO.
We obtain a neural network N that implicitly represents the visual-language bias in its weights.

P (C|I, T ) is used to select, for an image and an original caption, the hardest foil among all the possible foil captions, viz., the one with the highest probability according to the dataset bias learned by N.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If Neuraltalk's bias modeling is imperfect or if 'hardest' as defined by its probability does not align with human perception of difficulty, the dataset might not be as challenging or diagnostically effective as intended.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The three proposed tasks (T1: classification, T2: detection, T3: correction) are a comprehensive and appropriate set of diagnostic tasks for evaluating fine-grained LaVi understanding.
supporting_evidence: Given this data, we propose three tasks based on widely accepted evaluation measures.

We have conducted three tasks aiming at understanding whether LaVi models can spot if there are mismatches between their coarse representations of language vs. visual inputs (T1); if their language representation is fine-grained enough to detect where the mismatch is (T2); if their visual representation is fine-grained enough so to be able to extract from it the information necessary to correct the foil (T3).

By associating the dataset with a series of tasks, we allow for diagnosing various failures of current LaVi systems, from their coarse understanding of the correspondences between text and vision to their grasp of language and image structure.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If critical aspects of fine-grained LaVi understanding are not covered by these tasks, the diagnostic analysis might be incomplete.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The VQA models evaluated (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt) are representative of state-of-the-art LaVi models for the purpose of diagnosing fine-grained understanding.
supporting_evidence: We evaluate two state-of-the-art models: the popular VQA system proposed by Antol et al. (2015); Lu et al. (2015), and the attention-based model by Lu et al. (2016).
Therefore we have evaluated VQA models. In particular, we have used two of the three models evaluated in (Goyal et al., 2016) against a balanced VQA dataset.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If other state-of-the-art models, particularly those not primarily VQA-focused or with different architectural choices, perform significantly better, the generalizability of the diagnostic findings might be limited.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The computational constraint of selecting correction words from a limited set of target words (T3) does not fundamentally alter the diagnostic value of the task regarding visual representation capabilities.
supporting_evidence: For computational reasons, we have instantiated this task by asking models to correct the foil word by selecting the correct word from the target words, instead of from the whole dataset vocabulary (viz. more that 10K words).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the models' inability to correct is primarily due to the limited search space rather than a fundamental lack of visual representation, the conclusion about 'poor visual representation' might be partially misattributed.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The linguistic variables (Word2Vec similarity, word frequency, caption length) used in the mixed-effect logistic regression are sufficient and appropriate for diagnosing the underlying causes of model failures in T1.
supporting_evidence: We performed a mixed-effect logistic regression analysis in order to check whether the performance of the models in T1 can be predicted by various linguistic variables (see results in Figure 3). We included: 1) semantic similarity between the original word and the foil (computed as the cosine between the two corresponding Word2Vec embeddings); 2) frequency of original word in FOIL-COCO captions; 3) frequency of the foil word in FOIL-COCO captions; 4) length of the caption (number of words).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If other unmeasured linguistic or visual features significantly influence model performance, the diagnostic analysis might be incomplete or misattribute causes of failure.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The low correlation between object detection precision and model accuracy on T1, despite using different object detection models, is indicative that other challenges (beyond object detection difficulty) are the primary drivers of poor performance in the tested LaVi systems.
supporting_evidence: Indeed, there is low correlation between object detection precision and model accuracy (Pearson 0.0363 for the LSTM + norm I, 0.179 for HieCoAtt on Task 1).

While this is only an indicative result (because the models used for object detection are different from the endto-end VQA models tested here), we can assume that other challenges lower the performance of the tested systems.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the object detection models used for correlation analysis are not sufficiently representative or if the correlation metric is insufficient, the conclusion about the dominance of 'other challenges' might be premature.

argument_focus: Diagnostic evaluation of Language and Vision (LaVi) models' fine-grained understanding.

uncertainty_flags: The paper acknowledges that it remains unclear how results from existing VQA/IC tasks should be interpreted and what models are truly learning (Section 1, Lines 113-115).
The authors note uncertainty regarding whether current LaVi models truly capture vision and language in an integrative fashion (Section 2, Lines 205-207).
The paper explicitly states that the system by Ding et al. (2016) has not yet been evaluated against FOIL-COCO data (Footnote 1, Line 265).
The authors mention not evaluating Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (Fukui et al., 2016) against their tasks, though noting its higher accuracy in other benchmarks (Footnote 5, Lines 560-564).

The representativeness of human performance collected on a 'rather small subset' of the test set is acknowledged, though the authors express belief in its representativeness (Section 4.1, Lines 603-604).

The correlation between object detection precision and model accuracy is described as 'only an indicative result' due to using different models for object detection versus the end-to-end VQA models tested (Section 5, Lines 661-664).
chaining_notes: The paper explicitly positions its work as addressing three identified weaknesses in current VQA and IC research: triviality of tasks/language bias, lack of diagnostic capabilities, and inadequate evaluation metrics.

The FOIL-COCO dataset and its three associated tasks (classification, detection, correction) are presented as a novel diagnostic tool designed to reveal specific failures in fine-grained LaVi understanding.

The analysis section provides empirical evidence and specific diagnostic insights into *why* state-of-the-art models fail, linking performance to linguistic variables like semantic similarity and word frequency.

Future work is outlined to extend the diagnostic capabilities by requiring models to localize mismatches in images, which would move the research closer to textual/visual explanation and explainable AI.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a logically coherent argument for the inadequacy of current Language and Vision (LaVi) models in achieving fine-grained multimodal understanding. It effectively frames the problem by critiquing existing VQA and IC benchmarks for their inherent biases and lack of diagnostic capabilities. The proposed solution, the FOIL-COCO dataset, is systematically introduced with a detailed methodology for generating challenging, single-word 'foil' captions while mitigating language bias. The three diagnostic tasks are well-defined and progressively probe different levels of understanding. The empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art models, juxtaposed with human performance, provides strong evidence for the paper's central claim. The subsequent diagnostic analysis, linking model failures to specific linguistic and visual representational shortcomings, strengthens the overall argument by providing actionable insights into *why* models fail. The paper's structure flows seamlessly from problem identification to solution, experimentation, and detailed diagnosis, maintaining strong continuity and reinforcing its core message.
logical_argument_graph: Existing LaVi benchmarks (VQA, IC) are insufficient for diagnosing true fine-grained understanding due to language priors, conflated errors, and inadequate evaluation metrics. (C6, C7)
To address this, FOIL-COCO, a new diagnostic dataset, is created by extending MS-COCO with single-word 'foil' captions. (C2)
The FOIL-COCO generation process is designed to minimize visual-language bias by mining the 'hardest' foil captions using Neuraltalk. (C8)
Three diagnostic tasks (T1: classification, T2: foil word detection, T3: foil word correction) are proposed for FOIL-COCO, which are intuitive for humans. (C3, C9)
State-of-the-art LaVi models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt) are evaluated on these FOIL-COCO tasks. (Section 4.1)
Empirical results show that SOTA LaVi models perform poorly (near chance) on FOIL-COCO tasks, while humans achieve near-perfect performance. (C3)

Analysis of model failures reveals specific limitations: coarse representations, insufficient fine-grained language/visual understanding, and biases towards frequent/semantically similar concepts. (C4, C5)
Therefore, current LaVi models do not truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between language and vision. (C1)
This diagnostic framework can be extended to localize mismatches in images, moving towards explainable AI. (Section 6)

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset derived from MS-COCO, designed to evaluate the fine-grained interaction understanding of Language and Vision (LaVi) models. The core reasoning is that existing LaVi benchmarks suffer from language priors, conflated errors, and inadequate metrics, leading to models that perform well superficially without true multimodal integration. FOIL-COCO addresses this by creating 'foil' captions, which are original captions with a single, carefully chosen word replaced to create a subtle mismatch with the image. Three diagnostic tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, and foil word correction) are proposed and evaluated on state-of-the-art VQA models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt). The findings indicate that these models perform poorly, often near chance, while humans achieve near-perfect scores. The analysis further diagnoses specific failure modes, such as biases towards frequently occurring concepts and semantic similarity, and coarse representations of language and visual input. The methodology emphasizes minimizing language bias and creating challenging, diagnostically rich data.

S3: Design three diagnostic tasks (T1: classification, T2: detection, T3: correction) that are intuitive for humans (C9) and progressively test fine-grained understanding (A5).

identified_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art Language and Vision (LaVi) models do not truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between language and vision.
evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

We demonstrate that using language cues only is not enough to deal with FOIL-COCO and that it challenges the state-of-the-art by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image.
We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The state-of-the art LaVi models we have tested fall through that test, implying that they fail to integrate the two modalities.

evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

Our paper contributes to investigate these three weaknesses of current VQA and IC research by proposing an automatic method for creating a big dataset of real images with minimal language bias and some diagnostic abilities.
The dataset presented in this paper (Section 3) is built on top of MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014), and contains 297,268 datapoints and 97,847 images.
FOIL-COCO dataset is challenging.

identified_claims.claim_label: LaVi models perform poorly on FOIL-COCO tasks
identified_claims.claim_text: Current LaVi models perform poorly on three proposed tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction) on FOIL-COCO, often close to chance level, while humans achieve near-perfect performance.
evidence: We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The two state-of-the-art systems do significantly worse than humans on both T1 and T2.
They respectively only identify 34.51% (LSTM +norm I) and 36.38% (HieCoAtt) of the incorrect captions (T1).
On the foil word detection task, they only reach 24.25% and 33.69% accuracy (T2).
Their accuracy on foil word correction (T3) is extremely low, at 4.7% and 4.21% respectively.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

identified_claims.claim_label: Specific failures of LaVi models identified
identified_claims.claim_text: LaVi models exhibit specific failures: coarse representations of language and visual input, insufficient fine-grained language representation for mismatch detection, and poor visual representation for correcting foil words.
evidence: First, their coarse representations of language and visual input do not encode suitably structured information to spot mismatches between an utterance and the corresponding scene (tested by T1).
Second, their language representation is not fine-grained enough to identify the part of an utterance that causes a mismatch with the image as it is (T2).
Third, their visual representation is also too poor to spot and name the visual area that corresponds to a marked mistake in the text (T3).
The result on T3 makes it clear that systems are unable to extract from the image representation the information needed to correct the foil.

identified_claims.claim_label: LaVi models biased towards frequent/similar concepts
identified_claims.claim_text: LaVi models are biased towards frequently occurring concepts and struggle to distinguish related concepts when foil words are semantically similar to original words.
evidence: When the foil word (e.g. cat) is semantically very similar to the original one (e.g. dog), the models tend to wrongly classify the caption as ‘correct’.
The same holds for frequency values. In particular, the higher the frequency of both the original word and the foil one, the more the models fail.

This indicates that systems find it difficult to distinguish related concepts at the text-vision interface, and also that they may tend to be biased towards frequently occurring concepts, ‘seeing them everywhere’ even when they are not present in the image.

identified_claims.claim_label: Existing LaVi datasets have biases and conflate errors
identified_claims.claim_text: Current Language and Vision (LaVi) datasets, such as VQA and IC, suffer from language priors, dataset biases, and conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses.
evidence: Such results indicate that in current datasets, language provides priors that make it possible for a LaVi model to be successful without truly understanding and integrating language and vision.
Johnson et al. (2016) highlight a second weakness of such datasets, pointing out that “they conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses”.

Recent work has shown that the LaVi models are mainly based on language priors (Ren et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2016; Kafle and Kanan, 2016) and even simple correlation and memorization (Zhou et al., 2015; Jabri et al., 2016; Hodosh and Hockenmaier, 2016) can result in a good superficial performance, without the underlying models truly understanding the visual content.

Zhang et al. (2016) first unveiled that there exists a huge dataset bias in the popular VQA dataset by Antol et al. (2015): they showed that almost half of all the questions in this dataset can be answered correctly by using the question alone and ignoring the image completely.

identified_claims.claim_label: Existing IC evaluation metrics are inadequate
identified_claims.claim_text: Existing Image Captioning (IC) evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap, are only weakly correlated with human judgments, and fail to capture semantic propositional content.
evidence: it has been observed that existing IC evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap and that there is a need for measures that better substitute human judgments (Hodosh et al., 2013; Elliott and Keller, 2014; Anderson et al., 2016).

Elliott and Keller (2014) performed a sentence-level correlation analysis of NLG evaluation measures against expert human judgements in the context of IC. Their study revealed that most of those metrics were only weakly correlated with human judgements.
Anderson et al. (2016) showed that the most widely-used metrics for IC fail to capture semantic propositional content, which is an essential component of human caption evaluation.

identified_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO generation minimizes language bias
identified_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO dataset generation process, particularly the mining of the hardest foil caption using Neuraltalk, minimizes visual-language dataset bias.
evidence: To eliminate possible visual-language dataset bias, for each image and original caption, out of all foil captions generated in step 3, we selected only the hardest one.

We use Neuraltalk proposed in (Fei-Fei, 2015), one of the state-of-the-art image captioning systems, pre-trained on MS-COCO. Neuraltalk is based on an LSTM which takes as input an image and generates a sentence describing its content. We obtain a neural network N that implicitly represents the visual-language bias in its weights.
The ‘blind’, language-only model does badly on T1 with an accuracy of 43.95% (19.53% on foil captions), demonstrating that language bias is minimal.

identified_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive for humans
identified_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive to human beings, as evidenced by near-perfect human performance and simple annotation instructions.
evidence: We note as well that our task does not require any complex instructions for the annotation, indicating that it is intuitive to human beings (see §4).
Annotators are nearly perfect in classifying captions and detecting foil words.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The FOIL-COCO dataset and its associated diagnostic tasks represent a novel approach to evaluating fine-grained Language and Vision understanding. While there are comparable works on diagnostic datasets (e.g., CLEVR, Ding et al.), FOIL-COCO's specific focus on single-word 'foil' errors, generated to be maximally challenging by leveraging model biases and semantic similarity, distinguishes it. The novelty lies in the precise, controlled perturbation of captions to isolate specific types of multimodal understanding failures, rather than a broad, general evaluation. This innovative design is distinct from methodological flaws, which pertain to the execution and interpretation of the chosen methodology.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If LaVi models were developed with explicit architectural components or training objectives designed for fine-grained mismatch detection and correction, they could potentially perform significantly better on FOIL-COCO.

If the training data for LaVi models included more examples of subtle visual-linguistic inconsistencies or negative examples (e.g., 'this is NOT a dog'), they might learn to distinguish related concepts more effectively.
If the models had access to more explicit grounding mechanisms that link specific words to visual regions, they could improve on tasks like foil word detection and correction (T2, T3).
If the 'hardest foil' mining process was further refined to align more closely with human perception of difficulty, the diagnostic insights could be even more precise.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset and associated tasks, designed to assess the fine-grained understanding of Language and Vision (LaVi) models. It extends existing paradigms by systematically introducing single-word 'foil' errors into MS-COCO captions, a refinement intended to overcome limitations of prior datasets such as language priors and conflated error sources. The paper's core reasoning is that current LaVi models exhibit superficial understanding, and a carefully constructed diagnostic dataset like FOIL-COCO, with its three tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction), can expose these weaknesses. The empirical evaluation demonstrates that state-of-the-art LaVi models perform poorly on these tasks, often near chance, while humans achieve near-perfect scores. The analysis further diagnoses specific failure modes, including coarse representations, bias towards frequent concepts, and difficulty distinguishing semantically similar concepts. This work incrementally but meaningfully refines the evaluation methodology for LaVi models, pushing the community towards more robust and truly integrative multimodal understanding.

To address these weaknesses, a new diagnostic dataset and tasks are needed to test fine-grained LaVi understanding.

Models are biased towards frequently occurring concepts and struggle with semantically similar foil words (C5).
Therefore, FOIL-COCO serves as an effective diagnostic tool to reveal fundamental limitations in current LaVi models' multimodal understanding.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper addresses a critical, emerging concern in Language and Vision (LaVi) research: whether current state-of-the-art models truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between modalities, or merely exploit dataset biases and language priors. It argues that existing datasets and evaluation metrics are insufficient for diagnosing these deeper issues. To disrupt this status quo, the authors introduce FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset derived from MS-COCO, which features images paired with both correct and 'foil' captions containing single-word errors. The dataset generation process is meticulously designed to minimize language bias by algorithmically selecting the 'hardest' foil captions using a pre-trained image captioning model. Three diagnostic tasks are proposed: caption classification (correct vs. foil), foil word detection, and foil word correction. Empirical evaluation on state-of-the-art LaVi models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt) reveals consistently poor performance, often near chance level, in stark contrast to near-perfect human accuracy. The paper further provides a diagnostic analysis, identifying specific failure modes such as coarse representations, difficulty distinguishing semantically similar concepts, and bias towards frequently occurring words. This work fundamentally challenges the perceived success of LaVi models and advocates for a new conceptual framework for evaluation that prioritizes true multimodal integration over superficial performance.
logical_argument_graph: Existing LaVi models and benchmarks (VQA, IC) are flawed, exhibiting language priors, dataset biases, and conflating error sources, thus obscuring true fine-grained multimodal understanding (C1, C6, C7).
A new diagnostic approach is needed to precisely probe fine-grained interaction and pinpoint specific model failures.
The FOIL-COCO dataset is proposed, extending MS-COCO with carefully constructed 'foil' captions (single-word errors) to create challenging diagnostic scenarios (C2).
The FOIL-COCO generation process actively mitigates visual-language dataset bias by mining the 'hardest' foil captions (C8).
Three diagnostic tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction) are designed to evaluate different facets of fine-grained understanding (C3, A5).
State-of-the-art LaVi models perform poorly on FOIL-COCO tasks, often at chance level, while humans achieve near-perfect scores, indicating a significant gap in true understanding (C3, C9, A1).

Analysis of model failures reveals specific weaknesses: coarse representations, insufficient fine-grained language for mismatch detection, poor visual representation for correction, and biases towards frequent/semantically similar concepts (C4, C5).

Conclusion: Current LaVi models fail to deeply integrate language and vision, necessitating a shift towards diagnostic evaluation and targeted architectural improvements to foster true multimodal understanding.

prior_stage_inputs: The paper presents a logically coherent argument for the inadequacy of current Language and Vision (LaVi) models in achieving fine-grained multimodal understanding. It effectively frames the problem by critiquing existing VQA and IC benchmarks for their inherent biases and lack of diagnostic capabilities. The proposed solution, the FOIL-COCO dataset, is systematically introduced with a detailed methodology for generating challenging, single-word 'foil' captions while mitigating language bias. The three diagnostic tasks are well-defined and progressively probe different levels of understanding. The empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art models, juxtaposed with human performance, provides strong evidence for the paper's central claim. The paper introduces FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset derived from MS-COCO, designed to evaluate the fine-grained interaction understanding of Language and Vision (LaVi) models. The core reasoning is that existing LaVi benchmarks suffer from language priors, conflated errors, and inadequate metrics, leading to models that perform well superficially without true multimodal integration. FOIL-COCO addresses this by creating 'foil' captions, which are original captions with a single, carefully chosen word replaced to create a subtle mismatch with the image. Three diagnostic tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, and foil word correction) are proposed and evaluated on state-of-the-art VQA models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt). The findings indicate that these models perform poorly, often near chance, while humans achieve near-perfect scores. The analysis further diagnoses specific failure modes, such as biases towards frequently occurring concepts and semantic similarity, and coarse representations of language and visual input. The methodology emphasizes minimizing language bias and creating challenging, diagnostically rich data.

The manuscript presents FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset and associated tasks, designed to assess the fine-grained understanding of Language and Vision (LaVi) models. It extends existing paradigms by systematically introducing single-word 'foil' errors into MS-COCO captions, a refinement intended to overcome limitations of prior datasets such as language priors and conflated error sources. The paper's core reasoning is that current LaVi models exhibit superficial understanding, and a carefully constructed diagnostic dataset like FOIL-COCO, with its three tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction), can expose these weaknesses. The empirical evaluation demonstrates that state-of-the-art LaVi models perform poorly on these tasks, often near chance, while humans achieve near-perfect scores. The analysis further diagnoses specific failure modes, including coarse representations, bias towards frequent concepts, and difficulty distinguishing semantically similar concepts. This work incrementally but meaningfully refines the evaluation methodology for LaVi models, pushing the community towards more robust and truly integrative multimodal understanding.

The paper addresses a critical, emerging concern in Language and Vision (LaVi) research: whether current state-of-the-art models truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between modalities, or merely exploit dataset biases and language priors. It argues that existing datasets and evaluation metrics are insufficient for diagnosing these deeper issues. To disrupt this status quo, the authors introduce FOIL-COCO, a novel diagnostic dataset derived from MS-COCO, which features images paired with both correct and 'foil' captions containing single-word errors. The dataset generation process is meticulously designed to minimize language bias by algorithmically selecting the 'hardest' foil captions using a pre-trained image captioning model. Three diagnostic tasks are proposed: caption classification (correct vs. foil), foil word detection, and foil word correction. Empirical evaluation on state-of-the-art LaVi models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt) reveals consistently poor performance, often near chance level, in stark contrast to near-perfect human accuracy. The paper further provides a diagnostic analysis, identifying specific failure modes such as coarse representations, difficulty distinguishing semantically similar concepts, and bias towards frequently occurring words. This work fundamentally challenges the perceived success of LaVi models and advocates for a new conceptual framework for evaluation that prioritizes true multimodal integration over superficial performance.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper effectively argues that current Language and Vision (LaVi) models lack fine-grained understanding, primarily by demonstrating their poor performance on the novel FOIL-COCO dataset and its associated diagnostic tasks. The core claims regarding the limitations of existing datasets (C6, C7) are strongly supported by extensive literature citations. The FOIL-COCO dataset's design, including its bias mitigation strategies (C8) and the intuitiveness of its tasks for humans (C9), is well-evidenced. The empirical results (C3) quantitatively confirm that state-of-the-art LaVi models perform significantly worse than humans, often near chance, on classification, detection, and correction tasks. The subsequent diagnostic analysis (C4, C5) provides specific, evidence-based insights into model failures, such as biases towards frequent and semantically similar concepts, and coarse representations. While the claims are largely well-supported, some aspects related to the generalizability of the evaluated models and the scope of the diagnostic tasks warrant careful consideration, as they introduce minor uncertainties in the breadth of the conclusions.

identified_claims.claim_label: LaVi models lack fine-grained understanding
identified_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art Language and Vision (LaVi) models do not truly grasp the fine-grained interaction between language and vision.
evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

We demonstrate that using language cues only is not enough to deal with FOIL-COCO and that it challenges the state-of-the-art by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image.
We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The state-of-the art LaVi models we have tested fall through that test, implying that they fail to integrate the two modalities.
uncertainty_flags: it remains unclear how the reported results should be interpreted and what those models are actually learning.
it is unclear whether they capture vision and language in a truly integrative fashion.

identified_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO dataset challenges SOTA LaVi models
identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed FOIL-COCO dataset, an extension of MS-COCO with correct and 'foil' captions (single-word mistakes), effectively challenges state-of-the-art LaVi models by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image.
evidence: We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks.

Our paper contributes to investigate these three weaknesses of current VQA and IC research by proposing an automatic method for creating a big dataset of real images with minimal language bias and some diagnostic abilities.
The dataset presented in this paper (Section 3) is built on top of MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014), and contains 297,268 datapoints and 97,847 images.
FOIL-COCO dataset is challenging.

identified_claims.claim_label: LaVi models perform poorly on FOIL-COCO tasks
identified_claims.claim_text: Current LaVi models perform poorly on three proposed tasks (caption classification, foil word detection, foil word correction) on FOIL-COCO, often close to chance level, while humans achieve near-perfect performance.
evidence: We show that those models perform close to chance level, while humans are capable of doing the task accurately (Section 4).
The two state-of-the-art systems do significantly worse than humans on both T1 and T2.
They respectively only identify 34.51% (LSTM +norm I) and 36.38% (HieCoAtt) of the incorrect captions (T1).
On the foil word detection task, they only reach 24.25% and 33.69% accuracy (T2).
Their accuracy on foil word correction (T3) is extremely low, at 4.7% and 4.21% respectively.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

identified_claims.claim_label: Specific failures of LaVi models identified
identified_claims.claim_text: LaVi models exhibit specific failures: coarse representations of language and visual input, insufficient fine-grained language representation for mismatch detection, and poor visual representation for correcting foil words.
evidence: First, their coarse representations of language and visual input do not encode suitably structured information to spot mismatches between an utterance and the corresponding scene (tested by T1).
Second, their language representation is not fine-grained enough to identify the part of an utterance that causes a mismatch with the image as it is (T2).
Third, their visual representation is also too poor to spot and name the visual area that corresponds to a marked mistake in the text (T3).
The result on T3 makes it clear that systems are unable to extract from the image representation the information needed to correct the foil.

identified_claims.claim_label: LaVi models biased towards frequent/similar concepts
identified_claims.claim_text: LaVi models are biased towards frequently occurring concepts and struggle to distinguish related concepts when foil words are semantically similar to original words.
evidence: When the foil word (e.g. cat) is semantically very similar to the original one (e.g. dog), the models tend to wrongly classify the caption as ‘correct’.
The same holds for frequency values. In particular, the higher the frequency of both the original word and the foil one, the more the models fail.

This indicates that systems find it difficult to distinguish related concepts at the text-vision interface, and also that they may tend to be biased towards frequently occurring concepts, ‘seeing them everywhere’ even when they are not present in the image.

identified_claims.claim_label: Existing LaVi datasets have biases and conflate errors
identified_claims.claim_text: Current Language and Vision (LaVi) datasets, such as VQA and IC, suffer from language priors, dataset biases, and conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses.
evidence: Such results indicate that in current datasets, language provides priors that make it possible for a LaVi model to be successful without truly understanding and integrating language and vision.
Johnson et al. (2016) highlight a second weakness of such datasets, pointing out that “they conflate multiple sources of error, making it hard to pinpoint model weaknesses”.

Recent work has shown that the LaVi models are mainly based on language priors (Ren et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2016; Kafle and Kanan, 2016) and even simple correlation and memorization (Zhou et al., 2015; Jabri et al., 2016; Hodosh and Hockenmaier, 2016) can result in a good superficial performance, without the underlying models truly understanding the visual content.

Zhang et al. (2016) first unveiled that there exists a huge dataset bias in the popular VQA dataset by Antol et al. (2015): they showed that almost half of all the questions in this dataset can be answered correctly by using the question alone and ignoring the image completely.

identified_claims.claim_label: Existing IC evaluation metrics are inadequate
identified_claims.claim_text: Existing Image Captioning (IC) evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap, are only weakly correlated with human judgments, and fail to capture semantic propositional content.
evidence: it has been observed that existing IC evaluation metrics are sensitive to n-gram overlap and that there is a need for measures that better substitute human judgments (Hodosh et al., 2013; Elliott and Keller, 2014; Anderson et al., 2016).

Elliott and Keller (2014) performed a sentence-level correlation analysis of NLG evaluation measures against expert human judgements in the context of IC. Their study revealed that most of those metrics were only weakly correlated with human judgements.
Anderson et al. (2016) showed that the most widely-used metrics for IC fail to capture semantic propositional content, which is an essential component of human caption evaluation.

identified_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO generation minimizes language bias
identified_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO dataset generation process, particularly the mining of the hardest foil caption using Neuraltalk, minimizes visual-language dataset bias.
evidence: To eliminate possible visual-language dataset bias, for each image and original caption, out of all foil captions generated in step 3, we selected only the hardest one.

We use Neuraltalk proposed in (Fei-Fei, 2015), one of the state-of-the-art image captioning systems, pre-trained on MS-COCO. Neuraltalk is based on an LSTM which takes as input an image and generates a sentence describing its content. We obtain a neural network N that implicitly represents the visual-language bias in its weights.
The ‘blind’, language-only model does badly on T1 with an accuracy of 43.95% (19.53% on foil captions), demonstrating that language bias is minimal.

identified_claims.claim_label: FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive for humans
identified_claims.claim_text: The FOIL-COCO tasks are intuitive to human beings, as evidenced by near-perfect human performance and simple annotation instructions.
evidence: We note as well that our task does not require any complex instructions for the annotation, indicating that it is intuitive to human beings (see §4).
Annotators are nearly perfect in classifying captions and detecting foil words.
uncertainty_flags: though, we have collected human answers only on a rather small subset of the test set, we believe their results are representative of how easy are the tasks for humans.

strengths.title: Insightful Diagnostic Analysis of Failure Modes
strengths.description: The mixed-effect logistic regression analysis effectively identifies specific linguistic variables (semantic similarity, word frequency) that predict model failures, providing concrete insights into *why* models struggle. This moves beyond mere performance reporting to actionable diagnosis.
evidence: For both LSTM + norm I and HieCoAtt, Word2Vec similarity, frequency of the original word, and frequency of the foil word turned out to be highly reliable predictors of the model’s response. The higher the values of these variables, the more the models tend to provide the wrong output.

This indicates that systems find it difficult to distinguish related concepts at the text-vision interface, and also that they may tend to be biased towards frequently occurring concepts, ‘seeing them everywhere’ even when they are not present in the image.

concerns.title: Limited Representativeness of Evaluated Models
concerns.description: The paper evaluates only two specific VQA models (LSTM + norm I, HieCoAtt) as 'state-of-the-art LaVi models'. While these were relevant at the time, the generalizability of the diagnostic findings to the broader and rapidly evolving landscape of LaVi models, especially those not primarily VQA-focused or with different architectural choices, is not fully established. The paper acknowledges not evaluating Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (Fukui et al., 2016), which had higher accuracy in other benchmarks.
evidence: We evaluate two state-of-the-art models: the popular VQA system proposed by Antol et al. (2015); Lu et al. (2015), and the attention-based model by Lu et al. (2016).

We have not evaluated the Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (Fukui et al., 2016) against our tasks, however in (Goyal et al., 2016) this model accuracy is higher than the HieCoAtt of 4.3% – which in the context of our results is a rather little difference.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the implications of evaluating a limited set of models more explicitly, perhaps by framing the conclusions as specific to the tested architectures rather than all 'current LaVi models'. Acknowledge the potential for different model families to exhibit different failure modes.

concerns.title: Scope of 'Fine-grained Interaction' Definition
concerns.description: The paper operationalizes 'fine-grained interaction' primarily through single-word noun replacements. While this is a valuable diagnostic, it might not encompass the full spectrum of fine-grained multimodal understanding, such as subtle grammatical errors, complex relational mismatches, or the understanding of negation. The diagnostic power is excellent for the specific error type, but the claim of 'truly grasping the interaction' might be slightly overstated if other fine-grained aspects are not covered.
evidence: We only introduce one error (or ‘foil’) per caption (i.e. the caption is ‘nearly’ correct). Specifically, we replace one word in the original caption with an incorrect one.
In contrast, the foil captions we propose only differ from the gold description by one word and are thus more challenging.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the specific scope of 'fine-grained interaction' being addressed by FOIL-COCO and its tasks, acknowledging that other types of fine-grained errors exist and could be explored in future work.

concerns.title: Computational Constraint on Correction Task (T3)
concerns.description: For the foil word correction task (T3), models are asked to select the correct word from a limited set of 'target words' rather than the entire vocabulary. This computational constraint, while understandable, means the task does not fully test a model's ability to *generate* the correct word from an open vocabulary. This could slightly affect the interpretation of the conclusion regarding 'poor visual representation for correcting foil words' (C4), as the task is simplified.
evidence: For computational reasons, we have instantiated this task by asking models to correct the foil word by selecting the correct word from the target words, instead of from the whole dataset vocabulary (viz. more that 10K words).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explicitly discuss how the constrained vocabulary for T3 might influence the interpretation of results, and perhaps suggest future work to explore open-vocabulary correction if computational resources allow.

concerns.title: Indicative Nature of Object Detection Correlation
concerns.description: The paper notes a low correlation between object detection precision and model accuracy on T1, concluding that 'other challenges' lower performance. However, it qualifies this as 'only an indicative result' because different models were used for object detection versus the end-to-end VQA models. This qualification weakens the certainty of the conclusion that object detection is not a primary bottleneck, leaving some ambiguity.
evidence: Indeed, there is low correlation between object detection precision and model accuracy (Pearson 0.0363 for the LSTM + norm I, 0.179 for HieCoAtt on Task 1).

While this is only an indicative result (because the models used for object detection are different from the endto-end VQA models tested here), we can assume that other challenges lower the performance of the tested systems.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: If possible, conduct a more direct analysis using the internal object detection capabilities (or lack thereof) of the evaluated VQA models, or acknowledge this as a stronger limitation on the diagnostic power of this specific correlation.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
